newsitem.title: FRANCE: No claim, few clues in bombing of Paris mosque.
newsitem.headline: No claim, few clues in bombing of Paris mosque.

text.p: A crude bomb exploded at a Paris mosque run by a liberal Moslem cleric on Monday, slightly injuring the caretaker and leaving police puzzling whether to suspect French racists or Islamic extremists.

No one claimed responsibility for the blast, which blew in the door of Al-Dawwa Mosque and shattered windows of nearby buildings along the Rue de Tanger in a district in northeastern Paris where many North African immigrants live.
Police sealed off the area after the blast at 4.30 a.m. (0330 GMT). The caretaker was taken to hospital with minor hand injuries. Two other people were treated for shock.
Police said the bomb, apparently a fire-extinguisher stuffed with explosives, had been hung on the door of the building.
"We have no clues yet to guide the inquiry," a police officer said.
It was the first attack at a Paris mosque since the shooting of an imam in 1995 heralded a wave of bombings by Algerian Islamic extremists. It also coincides with rising intolerance in France.
The far-right National Front, which wants to send home three million immigrants, has staged several marches in recent months against a plan to build an extension to the mosque.
Paris Mayor Jean Tiberi condemned the blast as a cowardly act and an attack on religious freedom. He pledged his full support to France's Moslem community.

"By attacking a place of prayer, the perpetrators of this odious act are trampling on freedom of worship, and showing a lack of respect for the principles of secularism and liberty, foundations of our society," Tiberi said in a statement.
Roger Madec, the Socialist mayor of the Paris district where the bomb exploded, denounced political opposition to the mosque.

"The Moslem community has the right to have a decent place of worship. I prefer a mosque in the open to one in garages and cellars," he said. The Socialist Party denounced the bomb and urged respect of all religions.
Dalil Boubakeur, head of the main Paris Mosque, said he regretted that the attack "comes in a climate of anti-Islamism and of mixed-up ideas that are a danger to public peace".
Record 12.7 percent unemployment has fuelled hostility to foreigners.
The head of Al-Dawwa mosque, Kechat Larbi, is known as a liberal who organised talks with members of other religions and with the local community.
Local residents said leaflets had been distributed in the area last week calling for a more traditionalist line.
A bomb planted by suspected Algerian Moslem militants killed four people in an underground train in Paris in December.
The Islamic militants, who accuse French authorities of backing Algeria's military rulers, claimed responsibility for a previous bombing wave in 1995 which killed eight people and injured almost 200.
Last December's bomb, and many of those in 1995, were explosives packed into hollowed-out gas canisters.
The 1995 wave of bombings was preceded by the killing of a Moslem cleric, Sheikh Abdel-Baki Sahraoui, in a nearby mosque.
Security has been tight in Paris since the bombs, with troops guarding railway stations and airports.
